title: ImageNet's army of labellers
hook: Modern AI vision was built on photos sorted by tens of thousands of online workers.
peek: To teach computers to see, the researcher Fei-Fei Li needed millions of photos labelled by hand. Her team found the people to do it on Amazon Mechanical Turk, and the dataset they built kick-started the deep learning boom.
lede: In 2007 the computer scientist Fei-Fei Li set out to build a picture collection big enough to teach machines what the world looks like. Labelling it with students would have taken many years. Instead her team turned to Amazon Mechanical Turk, a site that paid people small sums for quick online tasks. Tens of thousands of workers ended up sorting about 14 million images.

bullets.text: Li has said roughly 49,000 workers in 167 countries took part. Each was shown a batch of photos and asked whether a word like "husky" or "teapot" really described them, and several people checked each image to catch mistakes.
The labels came from WordNet, a dictionary-like database that groups English nouns by meaning. That gave ImageNet more than 20,000 categories, from everyday objects to dozens of dog breeds.

ImageNet was first presented as a poster at a computer vision conference in 2009, and many researchers saw little point in so much data. Li started a yearly contest built on a smaller slice of 1,000 categories.

In 2012 a neural network called AlexNet won that contest by a wide margin, cutting the error rate far below its rivals. The result is widely seen as the moment deep learning took off, and it depended on all those human clicks.
